Figure 7-24 shows the output after the button is clicked. The object that generated the event is the button that contains the text OK, and the type of event was generated by a mouse. You have seen many Click() methods in earlier chapters that had the same parameters, but you did not use them. As with any other method, you are never required to use the parameters passed in.

# Appreciating Scope in a GUI Form

When you create event-handling methods in a GUI application, you must constantly be aware of variables and constants are needed by multiple methods. When you declare a variable or constant within a method, it is local to that method. If a variable or constant is needed by multiple event-handling methods—for example, by two different Click() methods—the variables or constants in question must be defined outside the methods (but within the Form class) so that both Click() have access to them. When you write other methods, you can decide what arguments to pass in, but event-handling methods that are generated automatically with predefined sets of parameters, you cannot be as flexible in using them as you can with other methods you write. In Chapter 9, "Using Classes and Objects," you see many examples of variables declared within a class but outside methods: variables are called fields.

# Methods to be Nonstatic When Associated with a Form

In Chapter 1, you learned that the keyword static is used in Main() in console applications because the method is associated with its containing class and not an object. When you create a GUI application and generate a method, such as a Click() method associated with a Button on a Form, the keyword static does not appear in the header because the method is associated with an object—the Form from which the method-invoking events are generated. When you execute a GUI program using a Form, the program creates a Form object, and the methods associated with it are nonstatic. In the chapter "Using Classes and Objects," you will learn much more about the differences between static and nonstatic methods. For now, omit the word static when you create methods that are intended to be called by other nonstatic methods in your GUI applications. For example, if you create a Click() method that responds to clicks, it will be nonstatic by default because it is associated with an object that is a Form.
